newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers push to put "God" in Constitution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers push to put "God" in Constitution.

text.p: A group of lawmakers reopened a religious controversy on Tuesday, calling for the word "God" to be included in an amended U.S. Constitution and to allow prayer in public schools.

Addressing a House of Representatives judiciary sub-committee hearing on the Constitution, Oklahoma Republican Ernest Istook argued that the Constitution was a barrier to religious freedom and needed to be amended.
"We seek a constitutional amendment because the courts have left us no other choice," said Istook, who proposed the Constitutional change.

The amendment, which has sparked vibrant public debate on the state's role in religion, suggests changing the Constitution to secure "the people's right to acknowledge God according to the dictates of conscience."
It also proposes the right of people to pray on public property, including in government-owned schools. A key tenet of the Constitution is the separation of church and state.
Those against the amendment say the state should not meddle in religion and that prayer in schools would be an insult to parents and children from diverse backgrounds.

"This would disrupt the religious peace we have enjoyed for years," said Representative Robert Scott, a Virginia Democrat on the committee, adding that religious freedoms were guaranteed under the Constitution and did not need to be amended.

Tuesday's hearing coincided with the release of a report by the U.S. State Department on religious freedoms worldwide. The report stressed that religious liberty was central to American history and identity.
A host of court cases has been filed challenging religious issues ranging from nativity scenes in courthouses to banning religious references at school graduations.

"This (amendment) represents a consensus by those who share the public's belief that our courts have too often become hostile to religion, placing barriers to religious expression which do not exist for other forms of free speech," Istook told the hearing.

Similar Constitutional amendments have been discussed at committee levels before, and in 1971 the House rejected such a change. The Senate has held votes on it three times since 1966, but none of those bids succeeded.
It could be years before the proposal is voted on. After Tuesday's hearing the amendment may be considered by a full committee which must decide whether to send it to the House.
American Atheists Inc., a watchdog group for the separation of the church and state, said in written testimony to the hearing that the amendment would allow "special privileges" for religion.
"Not only is the zero-God world of Atheists ruled out by this clause, the multi-God world of polytheists is ruled out as well," said Ellen Johnson, president of the Atheist group.
Several congressmen said stipulating that prayers should be allowed at schools could open the door to such practices as animal sacrifice, which is a ritual in some religions.
"If we are to have equal access to all religions then the Satanic cults would have to be allowed," said Chet Edwards, a Texan Democrat.

Rev. Timothy McDonald of the Iconium Baptist Church told the hearing that cults, satanists and some white supremacist groups would be granted the right to enforce prayer on children under the amendment. "Instead of religion helping bring us together, religious conflict would drive us apart."
